newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Shells fired near Cambodian temple town.
newsitem.headline: Shells fired near Cambodian temple town.

text.p: Shells were fired west of the Cambodian town of Siem Reap just after dawn on Friday, residents said, but military officals said there had been no fighting.
"I can hear shelling in the distance," one resident told Reuters by telephone.
"It's far away, we can only hear the artillery," said another.
The town, near the Angkor Wat temple complex, is under the control of forces loyal to Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, who ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh on Sunday.

Military officials loyal to Hun Sen said there had been no fighting in the area. But one official, speaking by telephone from the town, said Hun Sen's forces were due to fly more ammunition into the town later on Friday.
The town was quiet but tense. "People are afraid," he said.
Forces loyal to Ranariddh operate in the countryside around the town. Khmer Rouge guerrillas also operate in the forests in the province.
Clashes were reported between the rival prime ministers' forces in the area on Tuesday as Ranariddh's troops withdrew from the town to link up with their comrades in the countryside.
General Mol Reup, military adviser to Hun Sen, told reporters in Siem Reap on Thursday that the Khmer Rouge had about 600 soldiers in the province.
The general denied that there had been any fighting between Hun Sen's and Ranariddh's forces.
Siem Reap and the Angkor Wat complex were calm during the afternoon on Thursday but residents said there had been some light shelling in the early morning hours outside the town.
Some townspeople have been lugging bedrolls to Angkor Wat in the evenings to sleep there, believing that no Khmer faction would dare attack the magnificent 12th century temple complex.
Cambodia's unwieldy coalition government collapsed in violence on Saturday when Hun Sen's forces moved against Ranariddh's men in the capital. Ranariddh had left the country the previous day.
Hun Sen declared Ranariddh's ouster on Sunday as his forces consolidated their grip on the city and its outskirts, pushing Ranariddh's men from their bases in and around the city.
Ranariddh urged the U.N. Security Council on Thursday not to recognise any government resulting from the weekend's coup and to freeze aid to Cambodia.
